correctness.rationale: On the error space H=1⊥, the kernel of a block projection consists of vectors vanishing on that block. Projection preserves the in-block coordinates and distributes their negative sum uniformly outside, verifying the displayed quadratic form. The phrase 'solution space' at RESULT.md line 28 means the ambient error space in the calculation; the actual consistent solution set is a point. Internal block contrasts give eigenvalues p_j for nonsingleton blocks. On the two-dimensional block-constant subspace the projection axes are normalized centered block indicators, and their squared mutual inner products are s_i s_j/[(m−s_i)(m−s_j)]. This verifies the stated determinant for the trace-one mean operator. With two singletons the opposite-singleton test and the large-block contrasts give min(x,m(1−x)/(2(m−1))) as an upper bound. Its unique maximum is t1; equal singleton masses make the tested unit vector an eigenvector of value t1, and the other mean eigenvalue is 1−t1. Conversely equality makes that test vector an eigenvector, and its mixed entry with the other mean direction is a nonzero multiple of the singleton mass difference. With one singleton the mean determinant is strictly decreasing in both large-block masses once both are at least 1/3: in the displayed notation K>B0,C0. At x=y=t2=(m+1)/(3m+1) the determinant equals t2(1−t2). The trace-one eigenvalue criterion and contrast lower requirements force these masses uniquely, and verify attainability. With no singletons all three contrasts bound the rate by min p; uniform masses attain 1/3 since the normalized projections of the orthonormal block indicators contribute at least the identity before multiplying by 1/3. Strict ordering and choosing the pair of singleton row indices yield the global classification and count, also at m=4 where only the two-singleton profile exists. value.rationale: This is a natural exact randomized projection design problem on a symmetric tight frame. At equal per-step cost, the sharp guarantee selects the most unbalanced partition and a unique nonuniform mass assignment, and the fixed-profile classification shows exactly which structural change improves the bottleneck. That qualitative design statement is more informative than the small asymptotic gain over uniform masses. It does not assert computational-cost, least-squares noise, or multistep optimality.
